s.u1.title: Something has to be vibrating
s.u1.blurb: Every sound you have ever heard started with something moving back and forth.
s.u2.title: How it gets to you
s.u2.blurb: The air carries the sound and does not travel with it. That distinction is the whole topic.
s.u3.title: Describing a wave
s.u3.blurb: Five quantities, and what each of them does to what you actually hear.
s.u4.title: How fast, and through what
s.u4.blurb: Sound needs something to travel in, and it goes faster through a solid than through air.
s.u5.title: Sound coming back
s.u5.blurb: It bounces like a ball, and that gives you echoes, reverberation and the stethoscope.
s.u6.title: Below and above what you can hear
s.u6.blurb: Twenty hertz to twenty thousand. Outside that range the sound is still there and you are not equipped for it.
ch11.u1.fork.predict.prompt: You strike a tuning fork and hold it gently against a table tennis ball hanging on a thread. What happens to the ball?
ch11.u1.fork.predict.o0: Nothing, because the fork is not moving
ch11.u1.fork.predict.o1: It is knocked repeatedly to one side
ch11.u1.fork.observe: Hold the ball still first, then bring the ringing prong up to just touch it.
ch11.u1.fork.explain:
The ball is kicked away, again and again, by a prong that looks perfectly still.

The prong is moving. It is moving back and forth hundreds of times a second, far too fast for your eye to follow, and each time it comes forward it strikes the ball.

Touch the prong with a finger and you feel the same thing as a tingle, and the sound stops, because your finger has taken the energy out of it. Dip it in water and the water is thrown out in a spray. Every one of those is the same fact: the fork is vibrating, and that is where the sound comes from.
ch11.u1.do.steps:
1. Strike one prong of the fork on a rubber pad, never on anything hard, and hold it near your ear.
2. Touch the ringing prong with a fingertip. Note what you feel and what happens to the sound.
3. Hang the table tennis ball on a thread so it hangs still.
4. Strike the fork again and bring one prong up to just touch the ball. Watch the ball.
5. Strike the fork once more and dip one prong into a beaker of water. Watch the surface.
6. Now dip both prongs in and compare.
ch11.u1.do.watch: Striking the fork on a hard edge damages it and gives a dull sound that is mostly the table. A rubber pad or a shoe sole is the whole difference between this working and not.
a.ch11-u1-do-1.title: Touch a tuning fork that is ringing
a.ch11-u1-do-1.blurb: You can hear it. Now find out what it is doing, with a finger, a hanging ball and a glass of water.
ch11.u1.vibration:
A tuning fork is the clean case, because it does one thing and does it visibly once you know where to look. Everything else that makes a sound is doing the same thing.

Pluck a stretched rubber band and you can watch it blur. A guitar string is the same. A drum has a stretched skin that moves up and down. A flute has no moving part you can see at all, and what is vibrating is the column of air inside it. A bee has no voice, and the buzz is its wings beating.

Your own voice comes from two small folds of tissue in your throat called the vocal cords. Put two fingers on your throat and hum, and you will feel them.

Sound is a form of energy, and it is produced when something is set vibrating. There is no exception to that. If you can hear it, something moved.
a.ch11-u1-read-2.title: Vibration, every time
ch11.u1.sort.bin.2: Something solid, moving as a whole
ch11.u1.sort.i0.label: A guitar
ch11.u1.sort.i0.why: The string is plucked and the body carries the sound out.
ch11.u1.sort.i1.label: A tabla
ch11.u1.sort.i1.why: The stretched skin moves up and down when it is struck.
ch11.u1.sort.i2.label: A flute
ch11.u1.sort.i2.why: Nothing you can see moves. The air inside the tube is what vibrates.
ch11.u1.sort.i3.label: A whistle
ch11.u1.sort.i3.why: Same as the flute, in a much shorter tube, which is why the note is so high.
ch11.u1.sort.i4.label: A temple bell
ch11.u1.sort.i4.why: The metal itself rings, which is why touching it stops the sound.
ch11.u1.sort.i5.label: A bee in flight
ch11.u1.sort.i5.why: Its wings beat a few hundred times a second, and that is the buzz.
ask.ch11-u1-sort-3.seeit.q: If everything that makes a sound is vibrating, why can I never see it happening?
ask.ch11-u1-sort-3.seeit.a:
Because of how fast it is, and your eye cannot keep up.

A note in the middle of your hearing is around 500 oscillations a second. Your eye resolves perhaps twenty or thirty changes a second, so a prong doing five hundred is a blur at best and looks perfectly still at worst.

You can get round it. Touch it and you feel the vibration as a tingle. Dip it in water and the water is thrown out, because the water is slow enough to show you what the prong is doing. A very low note is slow enough to see directly: pluck a thick rubber band loosely stretched and you can watch it move.
a.ch11-u1-sort-3.title: What is vibrating?
a.ch11-u1-sort-3.blurb: In every case something is moving back and forth. Name it.
ch11.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: What is needed for a sound to be produced?
ch11.u1.quiz.q0.f0: Right, with no exceptions. If you can hear it, something moved back and forth.
ch11.u1.quiz.q0.f1: Temperature affects the speed of sound. It does not produce any.
ch11.u1.quiz.q0.f2: Moving from place to place is not the same as vibrating. A thrown stone makes no sound of its own.
ch11.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: A tuning fork is ringing and you touch a prong with your finger. What happens, and why?
ch11.u1.quiz.q1.o0: The sound stops, because your finger takes the energy out of the vibration
ch11.u1.quiz.q1.f0: Right, and you feel the vibration as a tingle at the same moment.
ch11.u1.quiz.q1.o1: Nothing, because the prong is not moving
ch11.u1.quiz.q1.f1: It is moving, several hundred times a second. Too fast to see and easy to feel.
ch11.u1.quiz.q1.o2: The sound gets louder, because your finger adds to it
ch11.u1.quiz.q1.f2: A finger absorbs energy. It does not supply any.
ch11.u1.quiz.q2.prompt: What vibrates when a flute is played?
ch11.u1.quiz.q2.o0: The column of air inside the tube
ch11.u1.quiz.q2.f0: Right, which is why covering different holes changes the note.
ch11.u1.quiz.q2.o1: The metal of the tube itself
ch11.u1.quiz.q2.f1: The tube holds the air column in shape. It is not what is vibrating.
ch11.u1.quiz.q2.f2: The fingers change the length of the air column. They are not the source.
a.ch11-u1-quiz-4.title: Where sound comes from
ch11.u2.propagation:
A vibrating object needs something around it to carry the sound away. That something is called the medium, and it can be a solid, a liquid or a gas. Without one there is nothing to carry anything, which is why two people standing on the moon cannot hear each other speak however hard they shout.

Here is the part worth getting right. The particles of the medium do not travel from the object to your ear.

When the prong moves forward it pushes the air in front of it, squashing it into a region where the particles are crowded and the pressure is high. That region is called a compression. When the prong swings back it leaves a region behind it where the particles are spread out and the pressure is low, which is called a rarefaction.

Each particle nudges its neighbour and then returns to where it started. The nudge passes on; the particle stays put. What reaches your ear is a train of compressions and rarefactions, which is to say a travelling pattern of pressure, and not a delivery of air.

The same thing happens at the beach. The wave crosses the whole bay, and a floating coconut bobs up and down in one place while it goes past.
a.ch11-u2-read-1.title: The air carries it and does not go with it
ch11.u2.slinky.predict.prompt: You and a friend hold a stretched slinky between you. You give your end one sharp push towards your friend. What travels along the slinky?
ch11.u2.slinky.predict.o0: The end of the slinky you pushed travels all the way to your friend
ch11.u2.slinky.predict.o1: A squashed-up region travels along it while the coils stay where they are
ch11.u2.slinky.predict.o2: Nothing travels; the whole slinky just moves
ch11.u2.slinky.predict.o3: A sideways wiggle travels along it
ch11.u2.slinky.observe: Tie a short piece of ribbon to one coil near the middle and watch that one coil as the pulse goes past.
ch11.u2.slinky.explain:
A region where the coils are bunched up travels the whole length of the slinky. The marked coil moves forwards, then back, and ends where it started.

That is a longitudinal wave: the coils move back and forth along the same direction the disturbance is travelling. Sound in air behaves exactly like this, with air particles instead of coils.

If instead you had flicked your end sideways, the wiggle would have travelled along while the coils moved up and down across the direction of travel. That is a transverse wave, and water ripples and light are of that kind. Sound is not.
ch11.u2.do.steps:
1. Stretch the slinky along the floor between two people. Do not overstretch it.
2. Tie a ribbon to one coil near the middle so you can watch that coil alone.
3. Give one end a sharp push along the length of the slinky and let go.
4. Watch the bunched region travel, and watch the marked coil.
5. Now push and pull your end over and over, and watch a train of bunched and spread regions.
6. Finally, flick your end sideways instead and compare what travels.
ch11.u2.do.watch: A group that watches the far end instead of the marked coil will report that the slinky moved across the room. The marked coil is the entire experiment: keep everyone's eyes on it.
ask.ch11-u2-do-2.moon.q: Why can astronauts not hear each other on the moon?
ask.ch11-u2-do-2.moon.a:
Because there is nothing between them to pass the nudge along.

Sound needs a medium: particles close enough together to push on each other. The moon has essentially no atmosphere, so a vibrating object there pushes on nothing, and the vibration stays where it is.

Astronauts talk by radio instead, which is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium at all. Light and radio cross empty space perfectly well, which is why you can see the moon and not hear it.
a.ch11-u2-do-2.title: Push a slinky, do not throw it
a.ch11-u2-do-2.blurb: A slinky held at both ends. One sharp push, and you can watch a compression travel.
ch11.u2.sort.i0.label: Sound travelling through air
ch11.u2.sort.i0.why: Air particles move back and forth along the direction the sound is going.
ch11.u2.sort.i1.label: A slinky given a sharp push along its length
ch11.u2.sort.i1.why: The coils bunch and spread along the same line the pulse travels.
ch11.u2.sort.i2.label: Ripples on the surface of a pond
ch11.u2.sort.i2.why: The water moves up and down while the ripple goes outwards.
ch11.u2.sort.i3.label: A slinky flicked sideways
ch11.u2.sort.i3.why: The coils move across the direction of travel.
ch11.u2.sort.i4.label: Light
ch11.u2.sort.i4.why: And it is not a mechanical wave at all: nothing material is oscillating, which is why it crosses empty space.
ch11.u2.sort.i5.label: Sound travelling through steel
ch11.u2.sort.i5.why: The medium has changed and the kind of wave has not. Sound is longitudinal in every medium.
a.ch11-u2-sort-3.title: Along, or across?
a.ch11-u2-sort-3.blurb: The test is the direction the particles move compared with the direction the wave travels.
ch11.u2.quiz.q0.prompt: When sound travels from a bell to your ear, what actually moves from one to the other?
ch11.u2.quiz.q0.o0: The disturbance, as a pattern of compressions and rarefactions
ch11.u2.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Each particle nudges its neighbour and returns to where it started.
ch11.u2.quiz.q0.f1: A breeze is air moving. Sound is not, and a sound can travel against a breeze.
ch11.u2.quiz.q0.f2: Nothing leaves the bell. It stays exactly where it is while it rings.
ch11.u2.quiz.q1.prompt: Why is a sound wave called a longitudinal wave?
ch11.u2.quiz.q1.o0: The particles move back and forth along the direction the wave travels
ch11.u2.quiz.q1.f0: Right. Along, rather than across, which is what transverse means.
ch11.u2.quiz.q1.o1: It travels in a long straight line
ch11.u2.quiz.q1.f1: Sound goes round corners perfectly well. The word is about the particles, not the path.
ch11.u2.quiz.q1.f2: A wavelength can be long or short and the wave is longitudinal either way.
ch11.u2.quiz.q2.prompt: Two astronauts stand on the moon and shout at each other. What do they hear?
ch11.u2.quiz.q2.o0: Nothing, because there is no medium to carry the sound
ch11.u2.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Sound needs particles to pass the push along, and there are essentially none.
ch11.u2.quiz.q2.o1: A faint sound, because sound travels a little way in a vacuum
ch11.u2.quiz.q2.f1: It travels no distance at all without a medium.
ch11.u2.quiz.q2.o2: A very loud sound, because there is nothing to absorb it
ch11.u2.quiz.q2.f2: With nothing to carry it, there is nothing to absorb either.
a.ch11-u2-quiz-4.title: How sound travels
ch11.u3.lab.predict.prompt: The curve a textbook draws for a sound wave goes up and down. What are the air particles doing when the curve is at a peak?
ch11.u3.lab.predict.o0: Moving upwards, as the curve shows
ch11.u3.lab.observe: Watch the band of particles above the curve, and find what is happening under each peak.
ch11.u3.lab.explain:
A peak is a compression: the particles there are crowded together and the pressure is high. A trough is a rarefaction, where they are spread apart.

Nothing goes up or down. The curve is a graph of density against distance, and the vertical axis measures crowding, not height.

This matters more than it sounds. A student who reads the curve as a picture of something wiggling has quietly converted sound into a transverse wave, and will answer every later question about it wrongly and confidently.
ch11.u3.lab.t1.label: A low note: 150 hertz.
ch11.u3.lab.t1.asks: Count the compressions in the window. How far apart are they, and what is the wavelength reading?
ch11.u3.lab.t2.label: A high note: 700 hertz.
ch11.u3.lab.t2.asks: Many more compressions in the same window. Which reading went down as the frequency went up?
ch11.u3.lab.t3.label: Keep 700 hertz and push the amplitude up.
ch11.u3.lab.t3.asks: The note has not changed pitch. What has changed, in the picture and in what you would hear?
ch11.u3.lab.closing: Frequency decides the pitch and amplitude decides the loudness. The speed is fixed by the air, so a higher frequency has to mean a shorter wavelength.
ask.ch11-u3-lab-1.updown.q: If nothing goes up and down, why does every book draw it as a wave?
ask.ch11-u3-lab-1.updown.a:
Because a graph of crowding against distance happens to come out as a sine curve, and a sine curve is what a wave looks like.

The shape is real and the up-and-down is not. The vertical axis is density, or pressure, and a peak means crowded while a trough means spread out. Drawing it this way lets you read the wavelength straight off, which is exactly what it is for.

Water ripples and light genuinely do oscillate across the direction of travel, and for those the same picture is a picture. For sound it is a graph, and the two look identical on paper.
a.ch11-u3-lab-1.title: The curve is a graph, not a picture
a.ch11-u3-lab-1.blurb: A band of particles above, and the curve every textbook prints below. Both show the same wave at the same instant.
ch11.u3.quantities:
A sound wave is fully described by a few numbers, and each of them does something you can hear.

Frequency is the number of complete oscillations passing a point each second, written with the Greek letter nu. Its unit is the hertz, Hz, named after Heinrich Hertz. The brain reads frequency as pitch: higher frequency, higher note.

Time period is how long one complete oscillation takes, written T, in seconds. It is simply the frequency upside down: v = 1/T.

Amplitude is how far the density swings either side of its average value, written A. The brain reads amplitude as loudness: a table struck hard gives a bigger swing than the same table struck gently.

Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive compressions, or two consecutive rarefactions, written with the Greek letter lambda, in metres.

Speed is how fast a compression travels through the medium. For air it is about 344 metres per second at ordinary temperatures, and it is the same for every frequency: a flute and a violin played together arrive together.

Those last three are tied by one equation:

v = λν

Because the speed is fixed by the medium, raising the frequency has to shorten the wavelength. There is no choice about it.

One more, which has no formula here. Quality, or timbre, is what lets you tell a guitar from a flute playing the same note at the same loudness, and it is also how you recognise a friend's voice in a dark room.
a.ch11-u3-read-2.title: Five quantities
ch11.u3.calc.c0.prompt: A sound wave has a frequency of 2 kHz and a wavelength of 35 cm. What is its speed?
ch11.u3.calc.c0.trap: Leaving the wavelength in centimetres and answering 70,000. The metre is the SI unit here.
ch11.u3.calc.c1.prompt: How long does that wave take to travel 1.5 km?
ch11.u3.calc.c1.trap: Multiplying instead of dividing. A larger speed has to give a smaller time.
ch11.u3.calc.c2.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of a sound wave of frequency 220 Hz in a medium where the speed is 440 m/s.
ch11.u3.calc.c2.s0: v = λν, so λ = v over ν
ch11.u3.calc.c2.trap: Multiplying and answering 96,800. Wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency.
ch11.u3.calc.c3.prompt: A source has a frequency of 100 Hz. How many times does it vibrate in a minute?
ch11.u3.calc.c3.g0: ν = 100 Hz, which is 100 times a second
ch11.u3.calc.c3.trap: Answering 100. The hertz is already per second, and the question asks per minute.
a.ch11-u3-calc-3.title: Speed, wavelength and frequency
ch11.u3.sort.i0.label: The frequency is raised from 200 Hz to 800 Hz
ch11.u3.sort.i0.why: Pitch is how the brain reads frequency. Four times the frequency is two octaves up.
ch11.u3.sort.i1.label: The same table is struck harder
ch11.u3.sort.i1.why: A harder strike gives a bigger amplitude, and the pitch is the same.
ch11.u3.sort.i2.label: The amplitude is doubled and the frequency left alone
ch11.u3.sort.i2.why: Amplitude is the loudness handle and nothing else.
ch11.u3.sort.i3.label: The listener walks further away from the source
ch11.u3.sort.i3.why: The wave spreads out, so the amplitude that reaches the ear is smaller. The frequency is unchanged.
ch11.u3.sort.i4.label: A guitar and a flute play the same note equally loudly
ch11.u3.sort.i4.why: Same pitch, same loudness. What tells them apart is quality, which is a third thing.
ch11.u3.sort.i5.label: The time period is halved
ch11.u3.sort.i5.why: Halving the period doubles the frequency, because one is the other upside down.
a.ch11-u3-sort-4.title: Pitch, loudness or neither?
a.ch11-u3-sort-4.blurb: Each change does exactly one thing to what you hear. Say which.
ch11.u3.quiz.q0.prompt: Which property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
ch11.u3.quiz.q0.f0: Right. The faster the source vibrates, the higher the note.
ch11.u3.quiz.q0.f2: The speed is fixed by the medium and is the same for every note.
ch11.u3.quiz.q1.prompt: Which property determines how loud a sound is?
ch11.u3.quiz.q1.f0: Right. A bigger swing in density means a louder sound.
ch11.u3.quiz.q1.f1: That is the pitch. A high note and a low note can be equally loud.
ch11.u3.quiz.q1.f2: Wavelength follows from the frequency and the speed, and does not set loudness.
ch11.u3.quiz.q2.prompt: The frequency of a sound in air is doubled. What happens to its wavelength?
ch11.u3.quiz.q2.f0: Right. The speed is fixed by the air, and v = λν, so one has to shrink as the other grows.
ch11.u3.quiz.q2.f1: That would need the speed to quadruple, and the air does not allow it.
ch11.u3.quiz.q2.f2: Then the speed would have doubled, and the speed is a property of the medium.
a.ch11-u3-quiz-5.title: Describing a sound wave
ch11.u4.speed:
Sound is not instant. A flash of lightning and its thunder leave at the same moment, and the flash arrives at once while the thunder takes seconds. Light travels about a million times faster.

How fast sound goes depends on what it is going through. The pattern is worth holding on to: fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases.

In air at 25 degrees it is about 346 m/s. In sea water, about 1531 m/s. In steel, about 5960 m/s, which is seventeen times faster than in the air above it.

The reason is how closely the particles are packed. A nudge passes on quickly when the next particle is already almost touching, and slowly when it has to cross a gap first.

Temperature matters too, in the same direction. Warmer air carries sound faster: 331 m/s at zero degrees and 344 m/s at twenty-two. You are not expected to memorise the table, only the ordering and the reason for it.

Put a finger in one ear, press the other against a long iron railing, and have someone tap the far end. You will hear the tap twice, through the iron first and through the air after.
a.ch11-u4-read-1.title: Fastest where the particles are closest
ch11.u4.calc.c0.prompt: You see a flash of lightning and hear the thunder 5 s later. How far away was the strike? Take the speed of sound as 346 m/s.
ch11.u4.calc.c0.trap: Dividing instead of multiplying. Five seconds of travel at 346 metres a second is a long way.
ch11.u4.calc.c1.prompt: Two children stand at opposite ends of an aluminium rod and one taps the end. Sound travels at 6420 m/s in aluminium and 346 m/s in air. How many times sooner does the tap arrive through the rod?
ch11.u4.calc.c1.g2: The distance is the same for both
ch11.u4.calc.c1.s0: Time is distance over speed, and the distance cancels
ch11.u4.calc.c1.s1: So the ratio of times is the ratio of speeds, the other way up
ch11.u4.calc.c1.trap: Comparing the speeds and calling the answer 6074. The question asks how many times, which is a ratio.
ch11.u4.calc.c2.prompt: A sound wave travels at 339 m/s and has a wavelength of 1.5 cm. What is its frequency?
ch11.u4.calc.c2.s0: v = λν, so ν = v over λ
ch11.u4.calc.c2.trap: Leaving the wavelength in centimetres and answering 226. The answer matters: 22,600 Hz is above the range a person can hear.
ask.ch11-u4-calc-2.hotday.q: Does an echo come back sooner on a hot day?
ask.ch11-u4-calc-2.hotday.a:
Yes, slightly, and that is a real effect rather than a trick question.

The speed of sound in air rises with temperature: about 331 m/s at zero degrees and about 344 m/s at twenty-two. On a hot afternoon it is faster still.

The cliff has not moved, so the distance is the same. A faster wave covers it in less time, and the echo comes back a little sooner. It is a few per cent, which is enough to matter in a measurement and not enough to notice by ear.
a.ch11-u4-calc-2.title: How long does it take
ch11.u4.quiz.q0.prompt: In which of these does sound travel fastest: air, water or iron?
ch11.u4.quiz.q0.f0: Right. The particles are closest together in a solid, so a nudge passes on soonest.
ch11.u4.quiz.q0.f1: Air is the slowest of the three, by a long way.
ch11.u4.quiz.q0.f2: Water is faster than air and far slower than iron.
ch11.u4.quiz.q1.prompt: Why is thunder heard several seconds after the flash is seen?
ch11.u4.quiz.q1.o0: Light travels very much faster than sound
ch11.u4.quiz.q1.f0: Right. They leave together and the light wins by a very long way.
ch11.u4.quiz.q1.o1: The thunder happens after the lightning
ch11.u4.quiz.q1.f1: They happen at the same instant. It is the arrival that differs.
ch11.u4.quiz.q1.o2: Sound is blocked by clouds and has to go round
ch11.u4.quiz.q1.f2: Clouds do not block sound, and going round would not account for seconds.
ch11.u4.quiz.q2.prompt: What happens to the speed of sound in air when the air gets warmer?
ch11.u4.quiz.q2.f0: Right. 331 m/s at zero degrees and 344 m/s at twenty-two.
ch11.u4.quiz.q2.f1: That is the direction for going from solid to gas, not for warming a gas.
ch11.u4.quiz.q2.f2: It changes by about four per cent across an ordinary day's range.
a.ch11-u4-quiz-3.title: Speed of sound
ch11.u5.echo:
Sound bounces off a hard surface the way a ball bounces off a wall. It follows the same laws as light: the incoming and outgoing directions make equal angles with the normal to the surface, and all three lie in one plane. The obstacle has to be reasonably large, and it can be rough or polished.

An echo is a reflected sound heard separately from the original. It is only heard separately if it arrives late enough, and the reason is in your head rather than in the air: the sensation of a sound lasts about 0.1 s in the brain, so anything arriving sooner merges with the original.

Take the speed of sound as 344 m/s. In 0.1 s it covers 34.4 m, and that has to be the round trip, there and back. So the reflecting surface must be at least 17.2 m away.

Closer than that and the reflection does not disappear. It arrives too soon to be separate and makes the original sound seem to drag on instead. That is reverberation, and in a large hall it builds up from many surfaces until speech becomes hard to follow. Auditoriums are lined with compressed fibreboard, rough plaster, heavy curtains and absorbent seats, all chosen to soak up sound rather than return it.

The rolling of thunder is reverberation on a much larger scale: one strike, reflected back and forth between clouds and ground.
a.ch11-u5-read-1.title: Echo, and why halls are built the way they are
ch11.u5.calc.c0.prompt: A person claps near a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. How far away is the cliff? Take the speed of sound as 346 m/s.
ch11.u5.calc.c0.s0: The sound travels to the cliff and back, so the 2 s covers twice the distance
ch11.u5.calc.c0.s1: Total path: 346 times 2, which is 692 m
ch11.u5.calc.c0.trap: Answering 692 and forgetting the return journey. Every echo question has that factor of two in it.
ch11.u5.calc.c1.prompt: An echo is heard 3 s after the shout. How far away is the reflecting surface? Take the speed of sound as 342 m/s.
ch11.u5.calc.c1.s0: Total path: 342 times 3, which is 1026 m
ch11.u5.calc.c1.trap: Forgetting to halve, again. It is the single most common slip in this topic.
ch11.u5.calc.c2.prompt: What is the shortest distance to a wall at which a distinct echo can be heard? Take the speed of sound as 344 m/s and the persistence of hearing as 0.1 s.
ch11.u5.calc.c2.g0: The echo must arrive at least 0.1 s after the original
ch11.u5.calc.c2.s0: In 0.1 s the sound covers 344 times 0.1, which is 34.4 m
ch11.u5.calc.c2.s1: That is the round trip, so halve it
ch11.u5.calc.c2.trap: Answering 34.4 and forgetting that half of it is the way back.
ask.ch11-u5-calc-2.multiple.q: Why does thunder roll on and on instead of being one bang?
ask.ch11-u5-calc-2.multiple.a:
Because it is being reflected, over and over, off clouds and hills and the ground.

A lightning strike is one event, and a very short one. What reaches you first is the sound that came straight to you. After that come copies of it that went to a cloud and back, to a hillside and back, to the ground and back, each arriving a little later and a little quieter.

It is the same thing a large empty hall does to a handclap, on a scale of kilometres rather than metres. A strike directly overhead on an open plain gives a single sharp crack, because there is almost nothing for it to bounce off.
a.ch11-u5-calc-2.title: Echoes
ch11.u5.sort.i0.label: A megaphone
ch11.u5.sort.i0.why: A cone that reflects the sound forward instead of letting it spread in all directions.
ch11.u5.sort.i1.label: A stethoscope
ch11.u5.sort.i1.why: The heartbeat reaches the doctor's ears by repeated reflection along the tube.
ch11.u5.sort.i2.label: The curved ceiling of a concert hall
ch11.u5.sort.i2.why: Curved so that sound reaching it is sent evenly to every corner of the hall.
ch11.u5.sort.i3.label: Heavy curtains on the walls of an auditorium
ch11.u5.sort.i3.why: Soft and thick, so sound hitting them does not come back as reverberation.
ch11.u5.sort.i4.label: Compressed fibreboard lining a hall
ch11.u5.sort.i4.why: The same job as the curtains, built into the walls.
ch11.u5.sort.i5.label: A soundboard placed behind a stage
ch11.u5.sort.i5.why: A curved board that catches sound going backwards and spreads it out over the audience.
a.ch11-u5-sort-3.title: Send it back, or soak it up?
a.ch11-u5-sort-3.blurb: Some designs are built to reflect sound on purpose, and some to stop it reflecting.
ch11.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: Why must a reflecting surface be at least about 17 m away for a distinct echo?
ch11.u5.quiz.q0.o0: Because the reflection must arrive at least 0.1 s after the original, and that is the round trip in that time
ch11.u5.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and the 0.1 s is a fact about your brain rather than about the air.
ch11.u5.quiz.q0.o1: Because sound cannot travel less than 17 m
ch11.u5.quiz.q0.f1: Sound travels any distance at all. It is the separation in time that is the issue.
ch11.u5.quiz.q0.o2: Because sound is too weak to reflect from closer surfaces
ch11.u5.quiz.q0.f2: A close surface reflects perfectly well. The reflection merges with the original.
ch11.u5.quiz.q1.o0: The persistence of a sound caused by repeated reflections
ch11.u5.quiz.q1.f0: Right, and it is why a large empty hall is hard to speak in.
ch11.u5.quiz.q1.f1: An echo is heard as a separate sound. Reverberation is the original dragging on.
ch11.u5.quiz.q1.o2: The gradual fading of a sound as it spreads out
ch11.u5.quiz.q1.f2: Spreading out makes a sound quieter. It does not make it last longer.
ch11.u5.quiz.q2.prompt: How is excessive reverberation in an auditorium reduced?
ch11.u5.quiz.q2.o0: By lining the walls and seats with sound-absorbing materials
ch11.u5.quiz.q2.f0: Right: fibreboard, rough plaster, heavy curtains and absorbent seats.
ch11.u5.quiz.q2.o1: By making the walls smoother and harder
ch11.u5.quiz.q2.f1: A smooth hard wall is a better reflector, which makes it worse.
ch11.u5.quiz.q2.f2: A larger hall gives sound further to travel and more surfaces to bounce off.
a.ch11-u5-quiz-4.title: Reflection of sound
ch11.u6.range:
A human ear responds to frequencies from about 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz. That is the audible range, and it is a fact about ears rather than about sound. Below and above it the waves are still there, still carrying energy, and you are simply not equipped to detect them.

Sound below 20 Hz is called infrasound. Rhinoceroses call to each other at frequencies as low as 5 Hz. Whales and elephants use it too, and it carries a long way. Earthquakes produce low-frequency waves before the main shock arrives, which may be why some animals appear disturbed beforehand.

Sound above 20,000 Hz is called ultrasound. Bats, dolphins and porpoises produce it, and bats use the echoes to find their way and to hunt in complete darkness. Some moths can hear the squeak of a bat and take evasive action, which is an arms race conducted entirely above our hearing.

The range narrows with age. Children under five, and dogs, hear up to about 25,000 Hz, and an adult's upper limit falls steadily. Nothing changed about the sound.

A hearing aid works inside the audible range. A microphone turns sound into an electrical signal, a battery-powered amplifier makes that signal larger, and a small speaker turns it back into sound at the ear.
a.ch11-u6-read-1.title: Twenty to twenty thousand
ch11.u6.sort.i0.label: 5 Hz, a rhinoceros calling
ch11.u6.sort.i0.why: Far below 20 Hz, and it carries over a long distance.
ch11.u6.sort.i1.label: 100 Hz, a man's speaking voice
ch11.u6.sort.i2.label: 4000 Hz, a whistle
ch11.u6.sort.i2.why: High, and still well within what an ear detects.
ch11.u6.sort.i3.label: 50,000 Hz, a bat hunting
ch11.u6.sort.i3.why: Well above 20,000 Hz, which is why the night sounds quiet to you.
ch11.u6.sort.i4.label: 22,600 Hz, a wave of wavelength 1.5 cm in air
ch11.u6.sort.i4.why: Just above the limit. Working out a frequency and then checking it against the range is a standard exam step.
ch11.u6.sort.i5.label: 15 Hz, waves ahead of an earthquake
ch11.u6.sort.i5.why: Below the limit, and animals that can detect it may act on it before people notice anything.
ask.ch11-u6-sort-2.dogs.q: Why can a dog hear a whistle that sounds silent to me?
ask.ch11-u6-sort-2.dogs.a:
Because the whistle is working above the top of your range and inside the top of the dog's.

A dog hears up to about 45,000 Hz and a person up to about 20,000. A dog whistle is built to sound at around 30,000 Hz, which lands neatly in the gap.

Nothing about the sound is unusual. It is an ordinary pressure wave of an ordinary loudness, and the only thing deciding who hears it is what the ear can respond to. A child of four would come closer to hearing it than you would, because the upper limit falls steadily with age.
a.ch11-u6-sort-2.title: Below, within, or above?
a.ch11-u6-sort-2.blurb: The audible range runs from about 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz. Place each one.
ch11.u6.ultrasound:
A high frequency means a short wavelength, and a short wavelength travels in a well-defined path instead of bending round obstacles. That one property is behind every use below.

Cleaning. Parts with awkward shapes, spiral tubes and electronic components, are put in a cleaning solution and ultrasound is sent through it. Dust, grease and dirt are shaken loose and fall off, including from places no brush reaches.

Finding flaws. Ultrasound is sent through a metal block used in a bridge or a machine. A crack inside reflects it back, and detectors on the far side see the shortfall. Ordinary sound is useless here, because its longer wavelength simply bends round the crack.

Echocardiography. Ultrasound reflected from the parts of a heart is used to build an image of it.

Ultrasonography. The same idea for the liver, gall bladder, uterus and kidneys, used to find stones and tumours, and to check a foetus during pregnancy. Reflections come from every boundary where the tissue density changes, and those are turned into a picture.

Breaking stones. Ultrasound can shatter small kidney stones into grains small enough to leave with the urine, which avoids an operation.
a.ch11-u6-read-3.title: What ultrasound is used for
ch11.u6.quiz.q0.prompt: What is the audible range of frequencies for an average human ear?
ch11.u6.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and the upper end falls as a person gets older.
ch11.u6.quiz.q0.f1: That would leave out most of the high notes anyone can hear.
ch11.u6.quiz.q0.f2: 200,000 Hz is far above what any human detects.
ch11.u6.quiz.q1.prompt: A sound of frequency 15 Hz is produced. What is it called, and can you hear it?
ch11.u6.quiz.q1.f0: Right. Below 20 Hz is infrasound, and a human ear does not respond to it.
ch11.u6.quiz.q1.f1: Ultrasound is above the range, not below it.
ch11.u6.quiz.q1.f2: It is infrasound, and it is below what an ear detects.
ch11.u6.quiz.q2.prompt: Why is ultrasound rather than ordinary sound used to find cracks inside a metal block?
ch11.u6.quiz.q2.o0: Its short wavelength travels in a well-defined path instead of bending round the crack
ch11.u6.quiz.q2.f0: Right. A longer wave simply goes round the defect and arrives at the detector as though nothing were there.
ch11.u6.quiz.q2.o1: It is much louder, so it penetrates metal better
ch11.u6.quiz.q2.f1: Loudness is amplitude and has nothing to do with it.
ch11.u6.quiz.q2.o2: Ordinary sound cannot travel through metal at all
ch11.u6.quiz.q2.f2: Sound travels through metal faster than through anything else.
a.ch11-u6-quiz-4.title: Hearing range and ultrasound
mis.heat-makes-sound.statement: Sound is produced by something being hot.
mis.heat-makes-sound.correction: Temperature changes how fast sound travels. It does not produce any. A vibration does.
mis.motion-makes-sound.statement: Anything moving from place to place produces sound.
mis.motion-makes-sound.correction: A thrown stone makes no sound of its own. The motion has to be a vibration, back and forth.
mis.fork-is-still.statement: A ringing tuning fork is not moving.
mis.fork-is-still.correction: It is moving hundreds of times a second, too fast to see and easy to feel with a fingertip.
mis.touching-adds-energy.statement: Touching a ringing fork makes the sound louder.
mis.touching-adds-energy.correction: A finger absorbs the energy of the vibration, which is why the sound stops almost at once.
mis.flute-tube-vibrates.statement: The metal of a flute is what vibrates when it is played.
mis.flute-tube-vibrates.correction: The column of air inside it does. That is why covering a different hole changes the note.
mis.fingers-make-the-sound.statement: The player's fingers produce the sound of a flute.
mis.fingers-make-the-sound.correction: They change the length of the vibrating air column. The air is the source.
mis.air-travels-with-sound.statement: The air itself travels from the source to your ear.
mis.air-travels-with-sound.correction: Each particle nudges its neighbour and returns to where it started. Only the disturbance moves along.
mis.source-particles-travel.statement: Particles leave the vibrating object and reach your ear.
mis.source-particles-travel.correction: Nothing leaves the bell. It stays exactly where it is while it rings.
mis.longitudinal-means-straight.statemen: Longitudinal means the sound travels in a straight line.
mis.longitudinal-means-straight.correcti: It describes the particles moving back and forth along the direction of travel. Sound goes round corners happily.
mis.longitudinal-means-long.statement: Longitudinal means the wave has a long wavelength.
mis.longitudinal-means-long.correction: A sound wave is longitudinal whether its wavelength is a centimetre or ten metres.
mis.sound-crosses-vacuum.statement: Sound can travel a short way through a vacuum.
mis.sound-crosses-vacuum.correction: It travels no distance at all. With no particles there is nothing to pass the push along.
mis.vacuum-makes-sound-louder.statement: Sound would be louder in a vacuum because nothing absorbs it.
mis.vacuum-makes-sound-louder.correction: With nothing to carry it there is nothing to absorb either, and nothing to hear.
mis.curve-is-a-wiggle.statement: The curve drawn for a sound wave is a picture of particles moving up and down.
mis.curve-is-a-wiggle.correction: It is a graph of density against distance. A peak means crowded together, not high up.
mis.amplitude-sets-pitch.statement: The amplitude of a sound wave determines its pitch.
mis.amplitude-sets-pitch.correction: Amplitude sets the loudness. Frequency sets the pitch.
mis.speed-sets-pitch.statement: The speed of a sound wave determines its pitch.
mis.speed-sets-pitch.correction: The speed is fixed by the medium and is the same for every note, which is why an orchestra arrives together.
mis.frequency-sets-loudness.statement: The frequency of a sound wave determines how loud it is.
mis.frequency-sets-loudness.correction: Frequency sets the pitch. A high note and a low note can be equally loud.
mis.wavelength-sets-loudness.statement: The wavelength determines how loud a sound is.
mis.wavelength-sets-loudness.correction: Wavelength follows from the frequency and the speed. Loudness comes from the amplitude.
mis.wavelength-follows-frequency.stateme: Doubling the frequency doubles the wavelength.
mis.wavelength-follows-frequency.correct: It halves it. The speed is fixed by the medium, and v equals wavelength times frequency.
mis.wavelength-is-fixed.statement: The wavelength of a sound in air is always the same.
mis.wavelength-is-fixed.correction: It changes with every note. Only the speed is fixed by the medium.
mis.sound-fastest-in-air.correction: Air is the slowest of the three states. Solids are fastest, because the particles are closest together.
mis.sound-fastest-in-water.correction: Water beats air and is far slower than a solid. Steel carries sound about four times faster than sea water.
mis.thunder-happens-later.statement: Thunder happens a few seconds after the lightning.
mis.thunder-happens-later.correction: They happen at the same instant. The light simply arrives about a million times sooner.
mis.clouds-delay-thunder.statement: Clouds block the thunder and delay it.
mis.clouds-delay-thunder.correction: Clouds do not block sound, and going round them would not account for seconds of delay.
mis.warm-air-slows-sound.statement: Sound travels more slowly through warm air.
mis.warm-air-slows-sound.correction: It travels faster: about 331 m/s at zero degrees and 344 m/s at twenty-two.
mis.temperature-does-not-matter.statemen: The speed of sound in air does not depend on temperature.
mis.temperature-does-not-matter.correcti: It changes by about four per cent across an ordinary day's range, which is enough to matter in a measurement.
mis.sound-needs-a-minimum-distance.state: Sound cannot travel distances shorter than about 17 m.
mis.sound-needs-a-minimum-distance.corre: It travels any distance. The 17 m is the shortest that lets a reflection be heard as a separate sound.
mis.close-surfaces-do-not-reflect.statem: A surface closer than about 17 m does not reflect sound.
mis.close-surfaces-do-not-reflect.correc: It reflects perfectly well. The reflection simply arrives too soon to be heard separately.
mis.echo-forgets-the-return.statement: The echo time multiplied by the speed gives the distance to the surface.
mis.echo-forgets-the-return.correction: It gives the whole journey, there and back. Halve it.
mis.reverberation-is-an-echo.statement: Reverberation and an echo are the same thing.
mis.reverberation-is-an-echo.correction: An echo is heard as a separate sound. Reverberation is the original one dragging on, from reflections arriving too soon to separate.
mis.reverberation-is-fading.statement: Reverberation is a sound fading as it spreads out.
mis.reverberation-is-fading.correction: Spreading makes a sound quieter. Reverberation makes it last longer, which is a different problem.
mis.smooth-walls-reduce-echo.statement: Smoother, harder walls reduce reverberation in a hall.
mis.smooth-walls-reduce-echo.correction: A smooth hard surface is a better reflector, so it makes reverberation worse. Soft and rough surfaces absorb.
mis.bigger-hall-reduces-echo.statement: Making a hall larger reduces its reverberation.
mis.bigger-hall-reduces-echo.correction: A larger hall gives sound further to travel and more surfaces to bounce off, which usually makes it worse.
mis.audible-range-too-narrow.statement: The audible range runs from about 20 Hz to about 2000 Hz.
mis.audible-range-too-narrow.correction: The upper limit is about 20,000 Hz. 2000 Hz is a perfectly ordinary high note.
mis.audible-range-too-high.statement: A human ear can hear up to about 200,000 Hz.
mis.audible-range-too-high.correction: That is ten times the real limit, and well into the range bats use.
mis.infrasound-and-ultrasound-swapped.st: Infrasound is above the audible range and ultrasound below it.
mis.infrasound-and-ultrasound-swapped.co: That is the two the wrong way round. Infra means below and ultra means beyond.
mis.infrasound-is-audible.statement: Infrasound can be heard if it is loud enough.
mis.infrasound-is-audible.correction: The ear does not respond to those frequencies at all. A rhinoceros calling at 5 Hz is inaudible to a person standing next to it.
mis.ultrasound-is-louder.statement: Ultrasound is used in industry because it is louder than ordinary sound.
mis.ultrasound-is-louder.correction: Loudness is amplitude, and has nothing to do with it. Its short wavelength is what lets it travel in a well-defined path.
mis.sound-cannot-cross-metal.statement: Sound cannot travel through a solid metal block.
mis.sound-cannot-cross-metal.correction: It travels through metal faster than through anything else, which is exactly why flaw detection works.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: What is needed before any sound can be produced?
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: Something has to be vibrating: moving rapidly back and forth. A tuning fork, a string, a stretched skin, a column of air or a pair of vocal cords.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'something has to move'. Moving from place to place is not enough: a thrown stone makes no sound of its own.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: You touch a ringing tuning fork with a finger and the sound stops. Explain why.
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: The prong was vibrating, and your finger absorbed the energy of that vibration. No vibration, no sound.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because the fork was never moving'. It was moving several hundred times a second, which is why the finger feels a tingle.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: Describe what actually travels from a ringing bell to your ear.
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: A disturbance: a train of compressions and rarefactions. Each air particle nudges its neighbour and returns to where it started. No air travels from the bell to you.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'the air travels to my ear'. That is a breeze, not a sound, and a sound can travel against a breeze.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: Why is a sound wave called a longitudinal wave?
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: Because the particles of the medium move back and forth along the same direction the wave is travelling, rather than across it.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because it travels in a long straight line'. Sound goes round corners perfectly well, and the word describes the particles.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Name the wave property that sets the pitch and the one that sets the loudness.
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: Frequency sets the pitch and amplitude sets the loudness. They are independent: a high note can be quiet and a low note can be deafening.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for them swapped. It is the commonest error in the chapter and the SWIFT word is there to hold them apart.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: Give the relation between the speed, the wavelength and the frequency of a wave, and say what follows from it.
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: v equals wavelength times frequency. The speed is fixed by the medium, so raising the frequency must shorten the wavelength.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for a claim that a higher note travels faster. Every frequency travels at the same speed in a given medium, which is why an orchestra stays together.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Put air, water and iron in order of the speed of sound through them, and say why.
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: Iron fastest, then water, then air. The closer the particles are to each other, the sooner a nudge passes on.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for air being put first. It sounds right because air is where we usually hear sound, and it is the slowest of the three.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: Explain why thunder is heard several seconds after the flash is seen.
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: They happen at the same instant. Light travels about a million times faster than sound, so the flash arrives effectively at once and the thunder takes seconds.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'the thunder happens later'. It does not. Only the arrival differs, and the gap is what tells you how far away the strike was.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: A person hears an echo 2 s after clapping. Describe how to find the distance to the cliff.
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: Multiply the speed of sound by 2 s to get the whole path, there and back, and then halve it.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for the halving being left out. It is the single most common slip in this topic and it doubles every answer.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: What is reverberation, and how is it reduced in a hall?
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: The persistence of a sound caused by repeated reflections from the walls, ceiling and floor. It is reduced by lining the surfaces with absorbent materials: fibreboard, rough plaster, heavy curtains and absorbent seats.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for reverberation and echo being treated as the same thing. An echo is heard separately; reverberation is the original dragging on.
recap.s.u6.q1.ask: State the audible range of frequencies for a person, and name what lies on either side of it.
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: About 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz. Below that is infrasound and above it is ultrasound.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Listen for infrasound and ultrasound the wrong way round. Infra means below and ultra means beyond, and the Latin is worth saying out loud once.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: Explain why ultrasound rather than ordinary sound is used to find cracks inside a metal block.
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: Its wavelength is very short, so it travels in a well-defined path. A longer wave bends round the crack and arrives at the detector as though nothing were there.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because it is louder'. Loudness is amplitude, and amplitude plays no part in this at all.
aid.s.u3.meaning: The five quantities that describe a sound wave, in a word that is itself about going fast. Two of them you can hear directly: frequency as pitch and amplitude as loudness. The other three follow from those two and the medium.
aid.s.u3.S.property: Swing of the density either side of its average: the amplitude
aid.s.u3.S.note: Written A. A bigger swing is a louder sound, and nothing else.
aid.s.u3.W.property: Wavelength, from one compression to the next
aid.s.u3.W.note: Written with the Greek letter lambda, measured in metres.
aid.s.u3.I.property: Interval that one complete oscillation takes: the time period
aid.s.u3.I.note: Written T, in seconds. It is the frequency upside down: v = 1/T.
aid.s.u3.F.property: Frequency, the oscillations passing a point each second
aid.s.u3.F.note: Written with the Greek letter nu, in hertz. Higher frequency, higher pitch.
aid.s.u3.T.property: Travel speed of a compression through the medium
aid.s.u3.T.note: About 344 m/s in air, and the same for every note, which is why an orchestra arrives together.
gloss.sound: A form of energy produced by a vibrating object and carried through a medium as a longitudinal wave.
gloss.vibration: Rapid to and fro motion. Every sound begins with something vibrating: a string, a skin, a column of air or a pair of vocal cords.
gloss.medium: The material a sound travels through, solid, liquid or gas. Without one there is nothing to pass the disturbance along.
gloss.compression: A region of a medium where the particles are crowded together and the pressure is high. Shown as a peak on the wave graph.
gloss.rarefaction: A region where the particles are spread apart and the pressure is low. Shown as a trough on the wave graph.
gloss.longitudinal-wave: A wave in which the particles of the medium move back and forth along the direction the wave travels. Sound is one in every medium.
gloss.transverse-wave: A wave in which the particles move across the direction the wave travels. Ripples on water are one; sound is not.
gloss.frequency: The number of complete oscillations passing a point each second, in hertz. The brain reads it as pitch.
gloss.hertz: The SI unit of frequency, equal to one oscillation per second. Named after Heinrich Hertz.
gloss.time-period: How long one complete oscillation takes, in seconds. It is the frequency upside down.
gloss.amplitude: How far the density of the medium swings either side of its average. The brain reads it as loudness.
gloss.wavelength: The distance between two consecutive compressions, or two consecutive rarefactions, in metres.
gloss.pitch: How high or low a note sounds. It is how the brain interprets the frequency of the wave.
gloss.loudness: How strong a sound seems to the ear. It follows the amplitude of the wave, and is a response of the ear rather than a property of the sound alone.
gloss.timbre: What lets you tell a guitar from a flute playing the same note equally loudly, and a friend's voice in a dark room.
gloss.echo: A reflected sound heard separately from the original. It needs a reflecting surface at least about 17 m away, because hearing persists for about 0.1 s.
gloss.reverberation: The persistence of a sound caused by repeated reflections from the surfaces of a hall. Reduced with absorbent materials.
gloss.audible-range: The frequencies a person can hear, about 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz. It narrows with age.
gloss.infrasound: Sound below about 20 Hz, too low for a person to hear. Rhinoceroses, whales and elephants use it.
gloss.ultrasound: Sound above about 20,000 Hz, too high for a person to hear. Its short wavelength travels in a well-defined path, which is what makes it useful.

path.guided.blurb: Every topic in the order the chapter builds them.
